title: Miami Hunters Return North of the Ohio
summary: To the Miami, whose towns lay north of the Ohio, northern Kentucky's forests, canebrakes and salt springs were places to hunt, trap and make salt.
bodyMarkdown:
To the [Miami](https://grokipedia.com/page/Miami_people), who call themselves Myaamiaki, "the downstream people," northern Kentucky was not home but part of a working landscape. Their towns lay north of the Ohio, along the Wabash and Maumee rivers. Kentucky's forests, canebrakes and salt springs were places to hunt, trap and make salt, and the people who used them knew the ground well.

That pattern grew out of upheaval. In the 17th century the [Beaver Wars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beaver_Wars), driven by Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) efforts to control the fur trade, pushed many nations out of the Ohio Valley and the southern Great Lakes. Archaeologist Jeannine Kreinbrink, writing in the [NKyTribune](https://nkytribune.com/2020/11/our-rich-history-newport-american-indian-overview-local-tribes-left-the-region-by-the-late-1600s/), reports that the local peoples who had lived there for thousands of years were gone by the late 1600s. The Miami themselves were displaced westward toward the Fox and Wisconsin rivers.

Peace changed the map again. After the [Great Peace of Montreal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Peace_of_Montreal) in 1701, which Miami leaders signed, the Miami moved south into the Wabash and Maumee valleys, closer to fur-rich country and French trading routes. Their towns, including [Kekionga](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kekionga) at the head of the Maumee, became centers of a wider world of trade and alliance. Wabash-valley relatives such as the Wea and Piankashaw lived downriver (see [Wea: Waayaahtanwa on the Wabash](/stories/wea-waayaahtanwa-on-the-wabash/)).

By the mid-1700s, the [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee), Miami and other Ohio and Indiana nations had extended their hunting territories back into northern Kentucky. Hunting parties used the Ohio and the [Licking River](https://grokipedia.com/page/Licking_River_(Kentucky)) country seasonally, returning north with hides and meat. For these nations the land was occupied and valuable, even without permanent villages on it.

Conflict followed as settlers moved into this hunting country. When settlement pressed north of the Ohio, Miami war leader [Little Turtle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Little_Turtle) led coalitions that defeated U.S. armies in 1790 and 1791 during the [Northwest Indian War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northwest_Indian_War). After defeat at Fallen Timbers in 1794, he endorsed the 1795 [Treaty of Greenville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Treaty_of_Greenville), which ended the war and began a long era of land cessions.

## Kentucky today

Removals between 1846 and the 1870s split the Miami into the federally recognized [Miami Tribe of Oklahoma](https://grokipedia.com/page/Miami_Tribe_of_Oklahoma) and the state-recognized [Miami Nation of Indiana](https://grokipedia.com/page/Miami_Nation_of_Indiana). According to [Grokipedia's history of the Miami people](https://grokipedia.com/page/Miami_people), the Myaamia Center, founded in 2001, now leads work to revive the Myaamia language, which keeps alive the voices of the hunters who once crossed the Ohio.
